name: Paul J. Crutzen
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Crutzen worked as a civil engineer and construction bureau employee through his mid-twenties, only beginning his academic career as a computer programmer at Stockholm University's meteorology department at age 26 in July 1959. His PhD came at 35 (1968) and Nobel Prize at 62 (1995).
early_history_summary: Crutzen graduated from a secondary school in Amsterdam in 1951 but his exam results did not qualify him for university scholarships. He studied civil engineering at a vocational school, then worked at a Bridge Construction Bureau in Amsterdam from 1954. After military service and marriage in 1958, he moved to Sweden and in July 1959 began work as a computer programmer at Stockholm University's Department of Meteorology, which opened the door to his academic career.
family_context_summary: Born in Amsterdam to Anna (Gurk) and Josef Crutzen. His parents were described as cosmopolitan and helped him become fluent in French, English, and German. The family experienced hardship during the German occupation and the 'winter of hunger' in the final months of WWII.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; parents were not scientists but were cosmopolitan and valued languages.
evidence_summary: Crutzen's path to chemistry was indirect: he could not afford university, trained as a civil engineer, and only entered academia at 26 as a computer programmer. His Nobel Prize-winning work on ozone depletion came decades later, with his PhD in 1968 at age 35. No material milestone is identifiable before age 26.

name: Margit Korondi
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold medal in uneven bars at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics at age 20, plus a team silver and four bronze medals in the same Games.
early_history_summary: Korondi was the daughter of a sports teacher and gymnastics coach, giving her early immersion in the sport. She competed for Hungary at the 1952 Helsinki Olympics at age 20, winning gold on uneven bars, a team silver, and four bronze medals across six events. She added two more Olympic medals at the 1956 Melbourne Games before defecting to the United States.
family_context_summary: Daughter of a sports teacher and gymnastics coach, providing direct domain exposure and coaching from childhood. Born in Celje, Yugoslavia, but competed for Hungary.
parent_family_domain_summary: Her father was a sports teacher and gymnastics coach, directly transferring domain expertise and early training access.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father-coach, gymnastics pipeline, Hungarian gymnastics system, early domain exposure
evidence_summary: Korondi's father was a sports teacher and gymnastics coach, giving her direct domain exposure and coaching from childhood. She benefited from Hungary's elite gymnastics pipeline, which produced multiple Olympic champions in this era. Her Olympic gold at 20 in uneven bars, plus five additional medals across two Olympics, demonstrates exceptional physical talent and early specialization. The family-domain apprenticeship through her father was the dominant early advantage.
starting_point: Born in Celje, Yugoslavia to a sports teacher and gymnastics coach father; family moved to Hungary where she trained in gymnastics from a young age.
current_position: Died on March 6, 2022 at age 89 in Los Angeles, California; had emigrated to the US after the 1956 Olympics and settled in Henderson, Nevada.

trajectory.event: Won Olympic gold medal in uneven bars at the Helsinki Olympics, plus a team silver and four bronze medals.
Won Olympic gold in team portable apparatus and silver in team all-around at the Melbourne Olympics, then defected to the United States.
Died on March 6, 2022 in Los Angeles, California.

name: Aleksandr Aleksandrovich Volkov
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Volkov was inspired by Gagarin's flight at age 13 and became a test pilot, but was not selected for the cosmonaut program until 1978 (age 30). His first spaceflight was in 1985 (age 37).
early_history_summary: Volkov was born in Horlivka, Ukrainian SSR. He witnessed Yuri Gagarin's spaceflight at age 13, which inspired him to pursue space exploration. He became a test pilot in the Soviet Air Force before being selected for the 1978 cosmonaut group at age 30. His first spaceflight to Salyut 7 was in 1985.
family_context_summary: Born in Horlivka, Ukrainian SSR, to a family of Russian ethnicity. Not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Volkov's path to space was through the Soviet military: he became a test pilot and was selected as a cosmonaut at 30. No material milestone is identifiable before age 26. His space career achievements all occurred well after 26.

name: Ali Hassan al-Majid
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; al-Majid rose through military ranks and nepotistic family connections to Saddam Hussein, with his first significant positions (Member of Regional Command) coming in 1982 at age 41 and Director of General Security in 1984 at age 43.
early_history_summary: Al-Majid was a cousin of Saddam Hussein and spent his early career in the Iraqi military. His rise to power came through family connections to the Ba'athist regime, with his first major appointments occurring in the early 1980s when he was already in his forties. He became notorious as 'Chemical Ali' for his role in the Anfal campaign against Kurds.
family_context_summary: Born into the Al-Begat tribal group from Tikrit; cousin of Saddam Hussein, which later provided his path to power. Early family background beyond this is not well documented.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond tribal/family connection to Saddam Hussein.
evidence_summary: Al-Majid's notoriety came from his role in the Anfal campaign and his execution in 2010. His rise was entirely nepotistic, dependent on his cousin Saddam Hussein's regime. No material milestone is identifiable before age 26; he was a military officer without documented distinction in his early career.

name: Vasyl Lomachenko
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic gold medal in featherweight boxing at the 2008 Beijing Olympics at age 20, awarded the Val Barker Trophy as the outstanding boxer of the tournament; also won European Championships gold the same year.
early_history_summary: Lomachenko was coached by his father Anatoly from a young age; his father, a boxing coach, first directed him through Ukrainian dance and gymnastics before allowing him into the ring. He built an extraordinary amateur record of 396 wins and 1 loss, winning World Championships gold in 2009 and 2011, and two Olympic gold medals (2008 and 2012). He turned professional in 2013 and became a three-division world champion in record time.
family_context_summary: Born in Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi, Ukrainian SSR; father Anatoly Lomachenko was a boxing coach who trained him from childhood, using an unconventional approach starting with dance and gymnastics before boxing.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Anatoly was a boxing coach who trained Vasyl from a young age, providing direct domain expertise and sustained individualized coaching throughout his career.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father-coach, boxing from childhood, gymnastics foundation, Ukrainian boxing pipeline, physical prodigy
evidence_summary: Lomachenko's father Anatoly was a boxing coach who trained him from childhood, first through dance and gymnastics to build athleticism before boxing. This father-coach relationship provided sustained, individualized coaching and direct domain immersion. Lomachenko's 396-1 amateur record, Olympic gold at 20 with the Val Barker Trophy, and subsequent record-setting professional career as a three-division world champion demonstrate exceptional physical talent and early specialization. The family-domain apprenticeship was the dominant early advantage.
starting_point: Born in Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi, Ukrainian SSR; father Anatoly was a boxing coach who trained him from childhood using an unconventional method starting with dance and gymnastics.
current_position: Retired from professional boxing in June 2025 at age 37; former three-division world champion (WBO featherweight, WBO super featherweight, unified WBA/WBO/WBC lightweight) and IBF lightweight champion; widely regarded as one of the greatest amateur boxers ever.

trajectory.event: Won Olympic gold in featherweight boxing at Beijing and was awarded the Val Barker Trophy as the tournament's outstanding boxer.
Won gold at the AIBA World Championships in Milan.
Won his second consecutive Olympic gold medal at the London Games, becoming a rare two-weight Olympic champion.
Won the WBO featherweight world title in his third professional fight, tying the record for fastest world title.
Became the fastest fighter to win world titles in three weight classes (12 fights), unifying the WBA and WBO lightweight titles.
Lost unified lightweight titles to Teofimo Lopez, his first decisive professional defeat.
Won the IBF lightweight world title by defeating George Kambosos.
Announced retirement from professional boxing in June 2025.

name: Graciela Iturbide
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Iturbide married at 20 and had three children, only turning to photography in 1970 at age 28 after the death of her daughter. Her first grant (W. Eugene Smith Grant) came in 1971 at age 29.
early_history_summary: Iturbide was born in Mexico City to traditional Catholic parents and was the eldest of thirteen children. She married architect Manuel Rocha Diaz in 1962 at age 20 and had three children. After her daughter Claudia died at age six in 1970, Iturbide turned to photography, studying at the Centro Universitario de Estudios Cinematograficos at UNAM under Manuel Alvarez Bravo, who became her mentor.
family_context_summary: Born to traditional Catholic parents in Mexico City; eldest of thirteen children. Her father took photographs of the family and gave her a camera at age 11. She married architect Manuel Rocha Diaz in 1962.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a casual photographer who gave her a camera at 11; no professional photography background in the family documented.
evidence_summary: Iturbide's photography career began at 28, triggered by the death of her daughter. Before 26, she was married with children and had no professional photography career. Her notable achievements, including the Hasselblad Award (2008), all came decades later. No material milestone is identifiable before age 26.

name: Leiji Matsumoto
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Matsumoto made his manga debut at 16 in 1954 with 'Mitsubachi no boken' in Manga Shonen magazine, but his big break came with 'Otoko Oidon' in 1971 at age 33. The early debut was a start but not a material career milestone.
early_history_summary: Matsumoto was born in Kurume, Fukuoka, the middle child of seven brothers. His father gave him a 35mm film projector and he watched American cartoons during the Pacific War. He started drawing at age six and manga at nine after seeing Osamu Tezuka's works. At 18, he moved to Tokyo to become a manga artist, debuting in 1954. However, his career did not take off until 1971 with Otoko Oidon.
family_context_summary: Born in Kurume, Fukuoka to a family of seven brothers. His father gave him a 35mm film projector in early childhood, exposing him to American cartoons and science fiction. The family was middle-class; no specific financial or domain advantages documented.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; father provided a film projector but no professional art or manga background is noted.
evidence_summary: Matsumoto debuted professionally at 16, but this was a modest beginning rather than a material milestone. His career languished for nearly two decades before his breakthrough with Otoko Oidon in 1971 at age 33. His iconic works (Space Battleship Yamato, Captain Harlock, Galaxy Express 999) all came after age 35. No material milestone is identifiable before age 26.

name: Trevor Noah
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Noah had small acting roles and a radio show from 2002, and was building a career as a South African TV host and comedian, but his breakthrough came with The Daily Show correspondent role in December 2014 (age 30) and host role in September 2015 (age 31). By 26 he was a working regional entertainer without a material milestone.
early_history_summary: Noah was born in Johannesburg to a Swiss-German father and Xhosa mother under apartheid, when their interracial relationship was illegal. He began with a small soap opera role in 2002, hosted a radio show on YFM, and started stand-up comedy at 21. By his mid-twenties, he hosted several SABC shows and the SAFTAs, but his international breakthrough came only after moving to the US in 2011.
family_context_summary: Born to a Swiss-German father and Xhosa mother in Johannesburg under apartheid; their interracial relationship was illegal at the time. Raised by his mother and grandmother in Soweto. Attended a private Catholic school. Multicultural upbringing shaped his comedy.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; parents were not in entertainment industry.
evidence_summary: Noah's career before 26 consisted of regional South African TV hosting and stand-up comedy. While he was steadily building recognition, no single material milestone stands out. His fame and major achievements (The Daily Show, Emmy Awards, Time 100) all came after age 30. The apartheid-era adversity of his upbringing shaped his comedic perspective but did not constitute a career milestone.

name: Yun Hyon-seok
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Yun died by suicide at age 18 on April 26, 2003. While he was active in LGBT activism and poetry as a teenager, his notability derives primarily from his death as a protest act, not from a material achievement during his lifetime.
early_history_summary: Yun was born in Incheon to two Catholic teachers. He began questioning his sexuality in middle school and faced bullying and homophobia. He joined poetry clubs and contributed writings, became a full-time employee of Solidarity for LGBT Human Rights of Korea in March 2003 at age 18, and became a conscientious objector to military service. He died by suicide on April 26, 2003, which sparked debate about homosexuality in South Korea.
family_context_summary: Born in Incheon to two teachers who were devout Roman Catholics. He faced homophobia from his family, who attempted to pressure him into being heterosexual and sent him to a psychiatric hospital in October 2002.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were teachers; no literary or activist domain background documented. Family homophobia was a source of adversity.
evidence_summary: Yun's brief life was marked by activism and poetry as a teenager, but his notability comes almost entirely from his death by suicide at 18 as a protest against anti-gay discrimination in South Korea. While his activism was meaningful, no independently verifiable material milestone was achieved during his lifetime that would qualify under the rubric. His Wikipedia notability (77 languages) stems from his death, not from a lifetime achievement.

name: András Adorján
milestone_by_age_26: Won the European Junior Chess Championship in 1969 at age 19, and finished runner-up in the World Junior Chess Championship the same year behind Anatoly Karpov; awarded the International Master title in 1970 at age 20 and Grandmaster title in 1973 at age 23.
early_history_summary: Adorján was born in Budapest as András Jocha and adopted his mother's maiden name at 18. He was trained by Bela Papp and showed early promise. In 1969, he became European Junior Champion at the Niemeyer Tournament in Groningen and finished runner-up in the World Junior Chess Championship in Stockholm behind Karpov. He earned the IM title in 1970 and GM title in 1973, the same year he won his first Hungarian Championship.
family_context_summary: Born in Budapest as András Jocha; adopted his mother's maiden name Adorján in 1968 at age 18. Family background beyond this is not well documented in reviewed sources.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no chess background in the family is noted, though he was trained by Bela Papp.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Hungarian chess tradition, Bela Papp training, Budapest chess culture, early competitive immersion
evidence_summary: Adorján emerged from Budapest's strong chess culture, trained by Bela Papp, and achieved European Junior Champion and World Junior runner-up at 19. The Hungarian chess ecosystem provided competitive infrastructure, but no significant family-domain advantage is documented. His early competitive immersion and dedicated training with Papp were the primary drivers. He later became a GM at 23, won the Hungarian Championship, and reached the Candidates quarterfinals in 1979.
starting_point: Born in Budapest, Hungary as András Jocha; family background not well documented beyond adoption of mother's maiden name at 18. Trained in chess by Bela Papp from a young age.
current_position: Died on May 11, 2023 at age 73 after a long illness; was a Hungarian chess Grandmaster, author of the 'Black is OK' book series, and former second to Garry Kasparov.

trajectory.event: Won the European Junior Chess Championship in Groningen and finished runner-up in the World Junior Chess Championship in Stockholm behind Anatoly Karpov.
Awarded the FIDE International Master title.
Awarded the Grandmaster title and won the Hungarian Championship (jointly).
Helped Hungary win the Chess Olympiad gold medal, ending the Soviet Union's 12 consecutive victories.
Qualified for the World Championship Candidates Tournament via the Riga Interzonal, reaching the quarterfinals.
Died on May 11, 2023 after a long illness.

name: Sofia Polgár
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 'Magistrale di Roma' tournament in 1989 at age 14, scoring 8.5/9 against several grandmasters with a performance rating of 2879, one of the strongest tournament performances in chess history; also won the World under-14 girls championship in 1986 and earned IM and WGM titles in 1990 at age 16.
early_history_summary: Sofia Polgár was born in Budapest into a Jewish family and was the middle of three sisters in father László Polgár's educational experiment to prove that children could achieve exceptional results if trained in a specialist subject from early childhood. She was homeschooled with chess as the focus. At 14, she stunned the chess world with the 'Sack of Rome' tournament performance, and earned IM and WGM titles at 16.
family_context_summary: Born into a Jewish family in Budapest; father László Polgár designed an educational experiment around chess, homeschooling all three daughters (Sofia, Judit, Susan) with chess as the specialist subject. The family also taught the daughters Esperanto.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father László Polgár was not a chess master himself but deliberately designed a childhood educational experiment centered on chess, proving his thesis that 'geniuses are made, not born.' He and wife Klára educated their daughters at home with intensive chess training.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Polgar experiment, father-educator, homeschool chess, sister peer team, Budapest chess culture, cognitive prodigy
evidence_summary: Sofia Polgár's early achievement was the product of father László Polgár's deliberate educational experiment: homeschooling with chess as the specialist subject from early childhood. The father served as dedicated coach, and the three sisters (Sofia, Judit, Susan) formed an exceptional peer team that multiplied learning. The 'Sack of Rome' at 14, with a 2879 performance rating against grandmasters, is one of the most remarkable tournament performances in chess history. The family-domain apprenticeship was the dominant and overwhelmingly documented early advantage.
starting_point: Born in Budapest, Hungary to a Jewish family; father László Polgár designed a deliberate educational experiment to train his three daughters as chess prodigies from early childhood, homeschooling them with chess as the specialist subject.
current_position: Hungarian-Israeli chess player, teacher, and artist living in Israel; married to GM Yona Kosashvili with two children; holds IM and WGM titles; largely retired from competitive chess.

trajectory.event: Won the World under-14 girls championship, finishing second overall to Joel Lautier.
Stunned the chess world by winning the 'Magistrale di Roma' tournament in Rome with 8.5/9 and a 2879 performance rating, known as the 'Sack of Rome.'
Awarded the FIDE International Master and Woman Grandmaster titles.
Finished second at the World Junior Chess Championship in Matinhos, Brazil.

name: Elias M. Stein
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26; Stein earned his PhD from the University of Chicago in 1955 at age 24 and began teaching at MIT, but this is a standard academic credential rather than a material independently verifiable achievement. His major mathematical contributions (Stein maximal principle, Tomas-Stein theorem, Fefferman-Stein theory) came later in his career.
early_history_summary: Stein was born in Antwerp, Belgium to Ashkenazi Jewish parents. The family fled to the United States after the German invasion in 1940. He graduated from Stuyvesant High School in 1949, where he was classmates with future Fields Medalist Paul Cohen, then attended the University of Chicago, earning his PhD in 1955 under Antoni Zygmund. He taught at MIT from 1955, moved to Chicago as assistant professor in 1958, and became a full professor at Princeton in 1963.
family_context_summary: Born in Antwerp, Belgium to Elkan Stein and Chana Goldman, Ashkenazi Jews from Belgium. The family fled to the United States after the German invasion in 1940, first arriving in New York City.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; parents were Belgian Jewish refugees with no documented mathematical background.
evidence_summary: Stein's PhD at 24 from the University of Chicago under Zygmund is notable but represents a standard academic credential rather than a material milestone. His major contributions to harmonic analysis, the Wolf Prize, and the National Medal of Science all came decades later. The refugee experience and Stuyvesant High School education provided early academic foundation, but no independently verifiable material milestone is identifiable before age 26.
